blurb: Every repo and skill from the 2 October issue, with what it does, who it's for, what you need and the exact setup steps from each project's own README.
intro: Issue #4 covered six trending GitHub repos and three new AI skills. Most are for people who already use a coding agent, and two are for specialists, so each section starts with who it's really for. If you only try two, start with Impeccable and Superpowers.

items.name: Impeccable
items.works_with: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Copilot and more
items.short: Makes your coding agent better at design, so sites stop looking AI-made.
items.what: A design skill with 24 commands, plus a checker with 61 rules, that steers your coding agent away from the generic look of AI-made websites (Inter everywhere, purple gradients, cards inside cards).
items.who: Anyone building websites or app screens with an AI coding agent: developers, indie hackers and designers who code.
needs: A coding agent. The README lists Claude Code, Codex CLI, Cursor, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot, OpenCode, Pi and others
Node.js for the installer. The npm package asks for Node 22.18 or later
No API key. The checker runs without an AI model

steps.title: Install from your project folder
steps.text: It detects which agents you use and asks whether to install for this project or everywhere. Reload your agent afterwards.

steps.title: Or, in Claude Code, use the plugin
steps.text: Then open /plugin and install Impeccable from the list.

steps.title: Or, in VS Code with Copilot

try.label: From the README
try.text:
/impeccable init

Then try:
/impeccable critique landing
/impeccable audit the header

(In Codex, type $impeccable instead. To check a folder without an agent: npx impeccable detect src/)

watch: The installer adds a design hook that runs the checker every time your agent edits a UI file. In Claude Code, hooks run even if you deny the command, so the first edit can download its engine. Install with `--no-hooks` if you don't want that.
In Codex you have to approve the hook in /hooks after installing or updating.
It saves working files to a `.impeccable/` folder. The README gives a `.gitignore` block so screenshots don't get committed.

items.name: Superpowers
items.works_with: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Copilot CLI, Pi and more
items.short: Skills that make your coding agent plan, test and review before it writes code.
items.what: A set of skills that switch on automatically and make your coding agent follow a proper workflow: brainstorm a spec, write a plan, write tests first, hand tasks to sub-agents, review the code, then finish the branch.
items.who: Anyone using a coding agent on a real project who wants it to plan and test before it starts typing. It's more than you need for quick one-off scripts.
needs: A supported coding agent. You install it separately in each one you use
Your agent's usual plan or API credits. Superpowers itself is free (MIT)

steps.title: Codex
steps.text: In Codex CLI run `/plugins`, search for superpowers and choose Install Plugin. In the Codex app, open Plugins in the sidebar and click + next to Superpowers.

steps.title: GitHub Copilot CLI
steps.code:
copilot plugin marketplace add obra/superpowers-marketplace
copilot plugin install superpowers@superpowers-marketplace

try.label: From the README
try.text:
Let's make a react todo list

If it's installed properly, the agent starts brainstorming with you before it writes any code.

watch: The README says the agent can work on its own for a couple of hours at a time, so expect long runs and heavy token use.
The test-first skill will delete code that was written before its tests. That can feel heavy for small jobs.
An optional visual helper loads a logo from the makers' site, which sends your Superpowers version. Set `SUPERPOWERS_DISABLE_TELEMETRY` to switch that off.

items.name: yoinks
items.short: Download a video from a link in your terminal, without ad-filled sites.
items.what: A terminal app where you paste a video link, pick a resolution or MP3, and it saves the file to your Downloads folder. The README says it works with YouTube, X, Instagram, Threads, TikTok and over 1,800 other sites.
items.who: Anyone happy to type one command in a terminal who's tired of ad-filled downloader websites. It isn't an AI tool.
needs: Node.js 18 or later
Nothing else. It downloads yt-dlp for you on first run, and uses ffmpeg if you have it (with a built-in fallback)

try.label: From the README
try.text:
yoinks <video link>

Or run yoinks on its own and paste a link when it asks. Pick a format with the arrow keys and press Enter. Esc goes back, Ctrl+C quits.

watch: The README says downloading can break a platform's terms of service. Only download what you have the right to keep.
Files always go to your Downloads folder. There's no option to change it yet, and playlists aren't supported.
The yt-dlp it downloads doesn't update itself yet, so sites may stop working over time. If you already have yt-dlp installed, yoinks uses yours.

items.name: Pi
items.short: A small, hackable coding agent for your terminal that works with many AI models. Version 1.0 shipped on 1 October.
items.what: A minimal coding agent for your terminal, like Claude Code or Codex CLI, that works with many AI model providers. You can extend it with skills, extensions, prompt templates and themes. Version 1.0 came out on 1 October 2026.
items.who: Developers who want one coding agent they can point at any model and customise. It deliberately leaves out sub-agents and plan mode, so it has fewer guardrails than the big-name agents.
needs: Node.js 22.19 or later. The Mac, Linux and Windows installers can install it for you
A subscription or API key from an AI provider. You connect it inside Pi with /login

steps.title: Start it in a project and log in
steps.text: Then type `/login` to connect your provider. Update later with `pi update`.

try.label: Suggested
try.text: Explain what this project does and list its main files.

watch: Pi has no permission system. It runs with your user's full access to files, programs and the network. For isolation, the README points to running it in a container.
The README invites you to publish your open-source sessions to Hugging Face. That's optional, and sessions can contain code and secrets.
The installer pipes a script into your shell. Read it first if you're unsure.

items.name: TileLang
items.short: A Python-style language for writing very fast GPU kernels.
items.what: A Python-style language for writing very fast GPU and CPU code, such as matrix multiplication and FlashAttention. It compiles to CUDA, ROCm, Metal and more.
items.who: GPU kernel and machine learning systems engineers who already know PyTorch and how GPUs work. It isn't a beginner tool, so most readers will just want to know it exists.
needs: Python 3.10 or later
PyTorch
A supported GPU: NVIDIA (the main target), AMD with ROCm, or an Apple Silicon Mac through Metal. The README's quick start uses an NVIDIA GPU

steps.title: On AMD, install a ROCm PyTorch first
steps.code:
pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/rocm7.0
pip install tilelang

try.label: From the README
try.text: Run the README's Quick Start: a short matrix multiply plus ReLU kernel that prints "GEMM + ReLU passed." For a gentler start, the README links examples/quickstart.py and the TileLang Puzzles repo (ten exercises that get harder as you go).

watch: Without a supported GPU, the quick start won't run as written.
Version 0.1.13 removed some older APIs. Read the compatibility notes before upgrading.
The CPU, CuTe DSL and WebGPU backends are experimental.

items.name: Cursor plugins
items.short: Cursor's official plugins, from GitHub and Gmail to HubSpot and Salesforce.
items.what: The official source for Cursor's marketplace plugins: about 85 plugins that bundle skills, rules, commands and connectors. They range from coding workflows to connectors for apps like Gmail, GitHub, HubSpot, Salesforce and Playwright. It's also the reference if you want to build your own.
items.who: Cursor users who want ready-made connectors and workflows, and developers who want to make and publish their own Cursor plugins.
needs: Cursor
An account with any app you connect, such as HubSpot or Salesforce. Some plugins ask you to sign in to that service

steps.title: Install from inside Cursor
steps.text: Cursor's docs: open Customize in the sidebar, find the plugin you want, select Install and choose whether it's for this project or for you everywhere. You can also browse cursor.com/marketplace.

steps.title: Or install from Agent chat
steps.text: Plugins can also be added by name in Agent chat. For example, the plugin that helps you build your own:

try.label: Suggested
try.text: Install the connector for an app you already use from Customize, then ask the agent a question about your data in it. If you build tools, try /add-plugin create-plugin, then /create-plugin with a name and what it should do.

watch: Some plugins can trade or move money, including Robinhood, Coinbase, eToro and X Money. Don't give an agent write access to financial accounts.
Connectors can read your email, CRM and files. Choose project or user scope carefully.
Cursor's docs say marketplace plugins are reviewed before listing. Plugins from other community sites aren't covered by that.

items.name: nano-banana
items.works_with: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, OpenCode
items.short: Makes slide decks and illustrations with Google's Nano Banana image models.
items.what: Plans a slide deck with you, then makes each slide as an image with Google's Gemini image models (Nano Banana). You review the slides in your browser, it redoes the ones you flag, and it packs everything into a PowerPoint file. It can also make figures and illustrations.
items.who: People who want their agent to make image-based slide decks or illustrations and are happy to pay for Gemini API use. The slides are images, so you can't edit the text in PowerPoint afterwards.
needs: A Google Gemini API key, set as `GOOGLE_API_KEY`. Google lists no free tier for these image models: roughly $0.07 to $0.24 per image
Python packages: `pip install pillow google-genai python-pptx python-dotenv`
A coding agent that supports skills

steps.title: Add the skills
steps.text: This installs all 16 EvoSkills, including nano-banana:

steps.title: Install the Python packages
steps.code: pip install pillow google-genai python-pptx python-dotenv

steps.title: Set your API key
steps.text: Put it in your environment rather than pasting it into chat, so it doesn't end up in transcripts.

steps.title: Fix the model names (important)
steps.text: As of 3 Oct 2026, the skill's scripts only accept three model names, and Google's deprecations page lists all three as shut down (two on 25 June 2026, one on 2 October 2026). Until the skill is updated, edit `SUPPORTED_MODELS` and `DEFAULT_MODEL` in `scripts/generate_ppt.py` and `scripts/edit_slide.py` to the replacement names Google gives: `gemini-3-pro-image` or `gemini-3.1-flash-image`. We haven't tested this fix with a live key.

try.label: Suggested
try.text:
Make me a 5-slide presentation on <your topic> in the Lineal Color style.

The skill asks about audience, length and language before it generates anything.

watch: Check the skill's GitHub page for an update to the model names before you start.
Every image is a paid API call. Regenerating the deck redoes every slide, and each edit is another call. A 12-slide deck on the Pro model is roughly $1.60 before edits.
It runs a small local web server (port 8080 by default) for reviewing slides. Stop it with `package_pptx.py --kill-server` when you're done.

items.name: ai-rulez
items.works_with: Claude, Cursor, Gemini, Copilot, Codex and 9 more
items.short: Write your AI rules once and keep every AI tool's config in sync.
items.what: A tool where you write your AI rules, context, skills and commands once in a `.ai-rulez/` folder, then it writes the right config files for each AI tool you use (CLAUDE.md, Cursor rules, Copilot instructions and so on). The skill teaches your agent how to run it.
items.who: Developers or teams using two or more AI coding tools on the same project who are tired of keeping their instructions in sync. It's overkill if you only use one tool.
needs: Node.js (for npx), or Python with uv, or Homebrew
No account or API key

steps.title: Try it without installing
steps.code: npx ai-rulez@latest init && npx ai-rulez@latest generate

steps.title: Or install it
steps.code:
brew install goldziher/tap/ai-rulez
npm install -g ai-rulez
uv tool install ai-rulez

steps.title: Add the skill to your project
steps.text: Then run `ai-rulez generate` to write it into each tool's skills folder.

try.label: From the SKILL.md
try.text:
ai-rulez add rule my-rule --priority high
ai-rulez generate --dry-run
ai-rulez generate
ai-rulez validate

watch: `generate` writes, and can remove, files across your tools' config folders. Run it with `--dry-run` first on an existing project so it doesn't overwrite a CLAUDE.md you wrote by hand.
Since version 4.22.0, rules go into each tool's own rules folder by default. Set `[rules] mode = "inline"` to keep them in the main files.
Includes and installed skills are fetched from remote git repos when you generate, so only use sources you trust.

items.name: uc-ai-file-analysis
items.works_with: Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI, opencode
items.short: Helps your agent send PDFs and images from an Oracle database to AI models.
items.what: Teaches your coding agent how to send PDFs and images stored in an Oracle database to AI models like Gemini or Claude, using the UC AI framework for PL/SQL. It also covers pulling text out of PDFs and images (OCR).
items.who: Oracle PL/SQL and Oracle APEX developers. It's no use without an Oracle database and the UC AI framework.
needs: Oracle Database 12.2 or later, and Oracle APEX
The UC AI framework installed in your database (see UC AI's installation docs)
An API key for your AI provider, and a model that accepts files. Provider usage is paid

try.label: Suggested
try.text: Using UC AI, write a PL/SQL block that sends the PDF in my_docs.blob_content where id = 1 to Gemini and asks for a one-paragraph summary.

watch: Big PDFs and high-resolution images use a lot of tokens, which costs money. Check the usage on each result.
